function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

REPLACE MODE (mode='replace', default): find a unique string and replace it. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, path, old_string, new_string.
PATCH MODE (mode='patch'): apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, patch.

mode.description: Edit mode. 'replace' (default): requires path + old_string + new_string. 'patch': requires patch content only.

path.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. File path to edit.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

{"content": "     1|# Week 8: Days 50-56 Postpartum
     2|
     3|## Body: Maternal Recovery & Breastfeeding/Pumping
     4|
     5|By week 8, your body has made remarkable progress in healing from childbirth. Most physical recovery from vaginal delivery or C-section is complete, though some changes continue. Lochia (postpartum bleeding) should have stopped by now—if you're still experiencing bleeding or spotting, consult your provider.
     6|
     7|**Breastfeeding & Pumping**: If you're breastfeeding, your supply is likely well-established and regulating to match your baby's needs. Many mothers notice their breasts feel softer and less "full" between feeds—this is normal and doesn't mean low supply. If you're pumping (especially if returning to work soon), aim to pump every 3 hours while separated from your baby to maintain supply. Store breast milk properly: fresh milk lasts 4 hours at room temperature, 4 days in the fridge, and 6-12 months in the freezer.
     8|
     9|> "I'm pumping 3 times a day at work and barely keeping up with demand" — Signal from r/breastfeeding
    10|
    11|**Physical Recovery Tips**:
    12|- Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels) continue to be important for long-term bladder control and sexual health
    13|- If you experience urinary leakage when laughing, sneezing, or exercising, you're not alone—1 in 3 women experience this postpartum
    14|- Gentle core strengthening (like pelvic tilts and heel slides) can help rebuild abdominal strength
    15|- Most providers give clearance for exercise and sexual activity around 6 weeks, but listen to your body
    16|- Monitor your energy levels—returning to work or increased activity may highlight lingering fatigue
    17|- Continue prenatal vitamins if breastfeeding; consider adding vitamin D if recommended by your provider
    18|- Hair shedding often peaks around month 3—this is normal postpartum telogen effluvium and should improve by month 6
    19|
    20|**Nutrition & Hydration**: Focus on nutrient-dense foods to support healing and milk production. Aim for:
    21|- Protein with every meal (lean meats, eggs, beans, Greek yogurt)
    22|- Complex carbohydrates for sustained energy (whole grains, sweet potatoes, oats)
    23|- Healthy fats for brain health (avocado, nuts, olive oil, fatty fish)
    24|- Plenty of fluids—breastfeeding increases thirst; aim for urine that's light yellow
    25|- Consider continuing prenatal vitamins while breastfeeding
    26|
    27|## Baby: Development & Care
    28|
    29|Your baby is now 2 months old—a milestone marked by increasing social engagement and emerging personality.
    30|
    31|**Developmental Milestones**: Around 8 weeks, many babies begin to:
    32|- Social smile in response to your face and voice (not just reflexive smiles)
    33|- Coo and make vowel-like sounds ("ah-goo", "ooh")
    34|- Follow objects and faces with their eyes
    35|- Hold their head up steadier during tummy time
    36|- Begin to push up on their forearms during tummy time
    37|- Show more controlled arm and leg movements
    38|
    39|**Sleep Patterns**: At 2 months, babies typically sleep 14-17 hours per day, but sleep is still fragmented. You might notice:
    40|- Longer nighttime stretches (possibly 4-6 hours for some babies)
    41|- More predictable nap patterns emerging
    42|- Increased alertness during wakeful periods
    43|- The "witching hour" (fussiness in late afternoon/evening) may still be present but often improves around this age
    44|
    45|> "My baby started sleeping 5-hour stretches at night and I feel human again" — Signal from r/NewParents
    46|
    47|**Feeding**: Your baby's stomach has grown significantly since birth. At 2 months:
    48|- Breastfed babies typically eat every 2.5-3 hours during the day (8-12 times in 24 hours)
    49|- Formula-fed babies may go slightly longer between feeds (3-4 hours)
    50|- Growth spurts can happen around 6 weeks and again at 8-10 weeks—expect cluster feeding for 2-3 days
    51|- Watch for hunger cues: rooting, hand-to-mouth, lip smacking (crying is a late sign)
    52|- Most babies at this age are eating 4-5 ounces per feeding if formula-fed
    53|
    54|**Health & Wellness**:
    55|- The 2-month well-baby visit typically includes first round of vaccines (DTaP, Hib, IPV, PCV13, Rotavirus)
    56|- Discuss any concerns about reflux, excessive spit-up, or unusual crying with your pediatrician
    57|- Tummy time is crucial—aim for 2-3 sessions per day, starting with 1-2 minutes and working up to 10-15 minutes total daily
    58|- Continue safe sleep practices: back to sleep, firm mattress, no loose bedding or soft objects in crib
    59|- Cradle cap (scaly scalp) is common and harmless—gentle brushing with a soft brush after shampooing can help
    60|
    61|## Mental Health: Beyond the Baby Blues
    62|
    63|By week 8, the baby blues (mood swings, tearfulness, irritability) should have resolved for most mothers. If you're still experiencing persistent sadness, anxiety, or overwhelm, it's important to evaluate further.
    64|
    65|**Postpartum Depression & Anxiety**: 
    66|- Postpartum depression affects approximately 1 in 7 mothers and can onset anytime in the first year
    67|- Postpartum anxiety is equally common and may present as constant worry, racing thoughts, or physical symptoms like dizziness or nausea
    68|- Risk factors include history of depression/anxiety, lack of support, traumatic birth experience, or breastfeeding difficulties
    69|- Symptoms to watch for: persistent sadness, loss of interest in activities, changes in appetite/sleep (beyond newborn care), feelings of worthlessness, difficulty bonding with baby, or intrusive thoughts
    70|
    71|> "I thought it was just tiredness, but I couldn't shake this heavy sadness" — Signal from Quora
    72|> "I worry something bad will happen to the baby all the time" — Signal from r/PostpartumDepression
    73|
    74|**Returning to Work Considerations**:
    75|- If you're planning to return to work soon, this transition can trigger anxiety and guilt
    76|- Start preparing 1-2 weeks before: practice pumping routine, do a trial run with childcare, prepare freezer meals
    77|- Communicate your pumping needs clearly with your employer (private space, reasonable break time)
    78|- It's normal to feel emotional about leaving your baby—many mothers experience this
    79|
    80|**Coping Strategies**:
    81|- Continue prioritizing sleep when possible—even short rest periods help
    82|- Maintain social connections—isolation worsens anxiety and depression
    83|- Consider joining a postpartum support group (virtual or in-person)
    84|- Practice self-compassion: you're adjusting to a monumental life change
    85|- Limit social media if it triggers comparison or inadequacy
    86|- Mindfulness or breathing exercises (even 2-3 minutes) can help regulate nervous system
    87|- If symptoms persist beyond 2 weeks or feel severe, reach out to your provider—treatment works and you deserve support
    88|
    89|## Partner Playbook: Supporting Week 8
    90|
    91|Your partner's role evolves as you establish routines and potentially prepare for work transitions. Their support remains crucial for your recovery and the family's adjustment.
    92|
    93|**If Returning to Work is Imminent**:
    94|- Help prepare and organize pumping supplies (bags, bottles, cooler, cleaning supplies)
    95|- Take on extra household tasks to free up your time for self-care or preparation
    96|- Listen to your concerns about leaving the baby and validate your feelings
    97|- Learn the baby's feeding cues and routines to feel confident during your absence
    98|- Consider taking a day off or working remotely your first day back to ease the transition
    99|
   100|**Daily Support Continues to Include**:
   101|- **Night Time**: Handle one waking if possible (bring baby to you for breastfeeding, then take for burping/diaper change)
   102|- **Feeding Support**: Burp baby after feeds, change diapers, bring you water and snacks during nursing/pumping sessions
   103|- **Household**: Manage meals, laundry, and cleaning—especially as you regain energy and may try to do too much
   104|- **Baby Bonding**: Encourage tummy time, talk and sing to the baby, wear baby in carrier for walks
   105|- **Emotional Check-Ins**: Ask specific questions ("How are you really feeling about pumping at work?" instead of "How are you?") and listen without jumping to fix things
   106|- **Self-Care Facilitation**: Encourage and protect time for you to shower, nap, or engage in activities that replenish you
   107|
   108|> "My partner took over all night feeds for a week so I could sleep—it changed everything" — Signal from r/Parenting
   109|
   110|## Call Doctor? Red-Flag Table for Week 8
   111|
   112||| Symptom | Normal | When to Call |
   113||---------|---------|--------|--------------|
   114|| **Bleeding (Lochia)** | Should have stopped by 4-6 weeks postpartum. Occasional spotting may occur. | Light spotting that resolves quickly; return of menstruation (especially if not breastfeeding). | Heavy bleeding (soaking more than one pad per hour), clots larger than a golf ball, foul odor, fever/chills, or bleeding that resumes after stopping. |
   115|| **Perineal/C-Section Pain** | Any discomfort should be mild and improving. C-section incision should be healed without signs of infection. | Mild tenderness, especially with prolonged sitting or activity. | Increasing pain, pus, redness, swelling, warmth around incision (C-section), foul odor, or pain that interferes with daily activities. |
   116|| **Breast Pain** | Breasts feel softer between feeds; occasional let-down sensation. Mild nipple sensitivity possible. | Breast fullness before feeds that softens after; occasional tingling during let-down. | Red streaks on breast, fever/chills/flu-like symptoms (mastitis), cracked/bleeding nipples that don't improve, persistent pain during/after feeds. |
   117|| **Baby's Feeding** | Predictable patterns emerging; baby content after feeds. | Steady weight gain (about 1-1.5 lbs/month), 6+ wet diapers/day, 3-4+ stools/day (breastfed), seeming satisfied after feeds. | Poor weight gain, lethargy, fewer than 6 wet diapers/day, projectile vomiting, bloody or mucousy stool, refusing multiple feeds in a row. |
   118|| **Baby's Sleep** | Longer nighttime stretches possible; more alert during day. | Sleeping 14-17 hours total, beginning to distinguish day/night, waking 1-3 times at night for feeds. | Extreme difficulty waking for feeds, limp or floppy appearance, breathing pauses >20 seconds, blue lips/face, fever ≥100.4°F. |
   119|| **Emotional Health** | Baby blues resolved; typical adjustment emotions present. | Occasional overwhelm, mild anxiety about baby, tears when tired, joy mixed with fatigue. | Sadness/hopelessness lasting >2 weeks, inability to enjoy baby, anxiety/panic attacks, thoughts of self-harm or harming baby, feeling detached from baby. |
   120|| **Urination/Bowel Movements** | Normal bladder and bowel function restored. | Regular urination without pain, bowel movements 3x/day to 3x/week (varies by individual). | Pain/burning with urination, inability to empty bladder, severe constipation with pain/blood, no bowel movement by day 4-5 postpartum (if not resolved earlier). |
   121|| **Fever** | None expected unless related to illness (cold, flu, etc.). | Low-grade fever (<100.4°F) possibly from mild illness or engorgement. | Temperature ≥100.4°F (38°C) — could indicate infection (uterine, mastitis, UTI, or other illness requiring treatment). |
   122|
   123|**Remember**: When in doubt, call your provider. It's always better to check—especially with concerning symptoms like fever, severe pain, or changes in baby's behavior or feeding.
   124|
   125|---
   126|
   127|*This week's guidance is based on:*
